abstract: ABSTRACT Metastasis is the leading cause of death related to breast cancer. Premetastatic niches (PMNs), which are remodelled by the primary tumours in distant organs, are essential for the colonisation of disseminated cancer cells. The vascular niche is among the most pivotal PMNs in breast cancer lung metastasis, and the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we report that breast cancer cells secrete dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (DPP3) via small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) to promote lung metastasis. Mechanistically, circulating DPP3 upregulates RAPGEF4 to activate the Rap1 signalling pathway in the lung endothelial cells through the DPP3–PFKP–YBX1 axis and promotes angiogenesis to remodel the vascular niche, thereby increasing lung metastasis. In addition, ARF4 recognises ISGylated DPP3, which facilitates its packaging into sEVs in breast cancer cells. Finally, treatment with losartan pharmacologically inhibits the ISGylation of DPP3, preventing its secretion via sEVs. In summary, our findings demonstrate that DPP3, which is encapsulated in sEVs and secreted by breast cancer cells, regulates angiogenesis in the lung and remodels vascular niches to promote breast cancer lung metastasis, making it a potential target for the diagnosis and treatment of breast cancer metastasis.

Materials and Methods
2.1
Ethical Statement
This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations. Specifically, human specimens were obtained from Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University (Wuhan, China) and approved by the Clinical Research Ethical Committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University in accordance with the principles of the Helsinki Declaration. Informed consent from all participants was obtained. All animal experiments were handled under the Guidelines of the China Animal Welfare Legislation and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the College of Life Science, Wuhan University.
2.2
Cells and Constructs
Cell lines, including MCF‐10A (CRL‐10317), MDA‐MB‐231 (HTB‐26), 4T1 (CRL‐2539) and HEK293T (CRL‐3216) used in this study, were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection and cultured in the recommended media or as indicated. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) were kindly gifted by Prof. Hanqiu Zheng (Tsinghua University). All cell lines were cultured in an atmosphere of 5% CO
2
in an incubator at 37°C. All cells used herein were tested to be free of mycoplasma contamination and authenticated using the short tandem repeat profiling method. Mycoplasma detection was tested by PCR with forward primer: 5’‐GGGAGCAAACAGGATTAGATACCCT‐3’ and reverse primer: 5’‐TGCACCATCTGTCACTCTGTTAACCTC‐3’ by MiniAmp thermocycler (Applied Biosystems, USA).
MCF‐10A cells were stably overexpressed with DPP3 (MCF‐10A/DPP3) or the empty PLVX‐IRES‐ZsGreen1 vector (MCF‐10 A/vec). MDA‐MB‐231/Lck‐GFP and MCF‐10A/Lck‐GFP cells were constructed by transfection of Lck‐GFP expression plasmid (Addgene #61099) and selected by G418 (Biofroxx, 1150GR001) and sorting of GFP
+
cells by flow cytometry. MDA‐MB‐231/Luciferase and 4T1/Luciferase cells were constructed by stably expressing plenti‐CMV‐Puro‐Luc (Addgene #17477) and selected by puromycin (BasalMedia, S250J0).
To construct knockdown cell lines, short hairpin RNA (shRNA) sequences targeted (Table
S8
) indicated genes were synthesised and cloned into pLKO.1 puro vector (Addgene, 8453). Cells were transduced by lentivirus and selected by puromycin (S250J0, Basal Media).
To knock out the DPP3 in MDA‐MB‐231 cells, using the CRISPR Cas9 genomic editing system, single‐guide RNA (DNA sequence GAAGGTGAGAACATCCAGGG) predicted by the CHOCHOP (
https://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/
) was synthesised in DNA form and annealed into double strands treated with T4 polynucleotide kinase and inserted into the lentiCRISPR‐v2 vector (Addgene, 52961). The constructed plasmid was transfected into MDA‐MB‐231 cells and selected by puromycin. Similarly, 4T1/DPP3‐KO cells using sgRNA (DNA sequence GCCGAGTGTTGTATGCACTG), 4T1/Rab27a‐KO cells using sgRNA (DNA sequence AGCGTCCCTGAAGAATGCAG). All knockout cell lines were screened by monoclonals and subsequently verified by Western blot.
As previously described (Wang et al.
2022
), the ZsGreen was added to the C‐terminal of DPP3 to construct the DPP3‐ZsGreen fusion protein. The DPP3 sequence and ZsGreen sequence were concatenated with the ScFv (Gly4Ser) x3 amino acid sequence coded by GGT GGA GGC GGT TCA GGC GGA GGT GGC TCT GGC GGT GGC GGA TCA as a linker.
To construct the reporters of YBX1‐mediated RAPGEF4 transcriptional regulation. The promoter region of human RAPGEF4 was cloned into the PGL3‐Basic reporter vector (Promega, Cat# E1751). P1 fragment using primers 5’‐TATGTTGCCCTGGCTGGTCT and 5’‐TGATTGCTGGTCAAGAACTA, P2 fragment using primers 5’‐CTGTAGTTCTTGACCAGC and 5’‐CCAAAAGCTTTCTGAAAATGC, P3 fragment using primers 5’‐TGACCTTGAAACATTCTCAGG and 5’‐CAGGCTGAAGTCACTGGC, P4 fragment using primers 5’‐GGGTCTCGGTTCTGCTGTGG and 5’‐GTTGAGCGGCGGCGCGCG and mutant of P1 (P1‐mut) fragment using primers 5’‐TCCCTAATCTACAGGACAGATCTATAGATTCGCTTTTTCTGGAAGTTTCAC and 5’‐AGCGAATCTATAGAtctgtcctgTAGATTAGGGATTGCCTAAGGCTGGG. For the overexpression vector construction, the human DPP3, YBX1, PFKP, UBA7, UBE2L6, USP18 and ISG15 were amplified from HEK293T cDNA and cloned into pLVX‐IRES‐ZsGreen1 and pLV3‐CMV‐MCS‐3×Flag‐Puro. Plasmids of potential ISGylation site mutants of human DPP3, dead mutants of human DPP3 and ISG15 and potential YBX1 binding site of RAPGEF4 promoter (P1‐mut) were created by site‐directed mutagenesis using 2×MultiF Seamless Assembly Mix (RM20523, ABclonal) according to the manufacturer's instructions. All plasmids were validated by sequencing (Quintarabio). All primer sequences for overexpression vector constructs are listed in Table
S4
.
2.3
Lentivirus Package
Plasmids such as shRNA, sgRNA or overexpression were transfected into HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine 2000 (Life Technologies) along with packaging plasmids: psPAX2 (Addgene, 12260) and pMD2.G (Addgene, 12259). Forty‐eight hours after transfection, the supernatant containing lentivirus was collected and filtered through a 0.45 µm filter. This filtered supernatant was then used to infect MCF‐10A, MDA‐MB‐231, 4T1 or HUVECs. The cells were incubated for 48 h in the presence of 10 µg/mL polybrene (Beyotime, C0351). Cells were selected based on puromycin or sorted by GFP
+
cells with FACS.
2.4
The sEV Isolation, Characterisation, Uptake and Treatment
The sEVs in the conditional medium were separated via ultracentrifugation as previously described (Yan et al.
2018
). Cells were cultured in an sEV‐free serum (prepared by ultracentrifugation serum at 100,000 ×
g
overnight [about 16 h] at 4°C) conditional medium, and the supernatant was collected and pre‐cleared by centrifugation at 500 ×
g
for 15 min and then at 10,000 ×
g
for 20 min. Eventually, the sEVs were isolated by ultracentrifugation at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min and then washed in PBS using the same ultracentrifugation conditions. The sEVs in the serum of mice or humans (breast cancer patients and healthy donors) were separated as previously described (Zhou et al.
2021
). The serum was diluted by an equal volume of PBS and centrifuged at 2000 ×
g
for 30 min at 4°C, followed by 12,000 ×
g
for 45 min at 4°C. Then, the supernatants were filtered through 0.22 µm filters (Millipore) and ultracentrifuged at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min at 4°C. The pellets were washed in PBS and subjected to a second ultracentrifugation step at 100,000 ×
g
for 70 min at 4°C. The mouse tumour‐derived sEVs were isolated following the protocol established previously (Hu et al.
2024
). Specifically, a ∼50‐mg piece of tumour was weighed and sliced on dry ice and then incubated in 100 U/mL collagenase type I in Hank's solution at 37°C. The dissociated tissue was spun at 300 ×
g
for 10 min at 4°C. The supernatant was transferred to a new tube and centrifuged at 2000 ×
g
for 15 min at 4°C. Cell‐free supernatant was filtered by a 0.22 µm filter gently and slowly to remove cell debris and spun at 10,000 ×
g
for 30 min at 4°C. The supernatants were ultracentrifugation at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min and resuspended in PBS for a second ultracentrifuged step at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min at 4°C.
OptiPrep (Sigma‐Aldrich, D1556) density gradient centrifugation was performed as previously described. EVs isolated by ultracentrifugation were loaded onto a 12‐step OptiPrep gradient consisting of 30%, 27.5%, 25%, 22.5%, 20%, 17.5%, 15%, 12.5%, 10%, 7.5%, 5% and 2.5% iodixanol in 20 mM Hepes (pH 7.2), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM Na
3
VO
4
and 50 mM NaF. After centrifugation in an SW 40 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter) at 110,000 ×
g
at 4°C for 16 h, twelve 1 mL fractions were collected and washed in PBS by another spin at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min before western blot analysis (Yan et al.
2018
). EVs' size distribution was analysed using a CytoFLEX nanoFlow cytometer according to the manufacturer's instructions. The cytometer was calibrated for gating EVs with bead mixtures (Lot #2692902 and #BA105). About 10
9
particles/mL of fresh EVs were diluted 10,000‐fold in PBS. The report for particle size was generated directly from the CytExpert 2.2 software. The sEVs were negatively stained and characterised by transmission electron microscope (TEM). The sEVs were resuspended in 0.22 µm filters in PBS, gently dropped on the copper grids for 1 min, then stained using 2% uranyl acetate (SPI‐Chem, #02624‐AB) for 30 s at room temperature. The grids were examined by a JEOL JEM‐1400 Plus transmission electron microscope, and images were analysed by GATAN GMS 3 digital micrograph software.
For the sEVs uptake assay, sEVs extracted from each cell line were labelled with CFSE (eBioscience, 65‐0850‐84). CFSE was added to the PBS‐suspended sEVs at 5 µM and incubated for 1 h at room temperature before the washing step. This was followed by an extra round of ultracentrifugation washing in PBS to remove the excess dye. HUVECs were seeded into a 6‐well plate and incubated with CFSE‐labelled sEVs for 24 h. Images were acquired using the Leica DMi8.
For cell treatment, 2 µg of sEVs (equivalent to those derived from ∼5 × 10
6
parental cells) based on protein measurement using the BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added to 2 × 10
5
recipient cells in one well of a 6‐well plate. Cells treated with indicated sEVs were harvested after 24 h for RNA extraction and after 48 h for protein samples.
2.5
RNA Extraction and RT‐qPCR
Total RNA from cultured cells or tissues was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, 15596026) followed by cDNA synthesis using the MonScript RTIII Super Mix with dsDNase Kit (Monad Biotech, 509 MR05201). A CFX Connect real‐time PCR system (Bio‐Rad Laboratories) was used to perform quantitative real‐time PCR (RT‐qPCR) of cDNA samples using MonAmp ChemoHS qPCR Mix (Monad Biotech, MQ00401). All primers were designed using PrimerBank, and sequences are listed in Table
S5
.
2.6
Western Blots
Cells and sEVs were lysed in NP‐40 buffer (50 mM Tris‐HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, EDTA, 1% Nonidet P‐40, phosphatase inhibitor, and protease inhibitor [Sigma, 11836153001]). The mouse tissues (∼20 mg per sample) were ground with radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer (50 mM Tris‐HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X‐100, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, sodium orthovanadate, sodium fluoride, EDTA and leupeptin, phosphatase inhibitor and protease inhibitor [Sigma, 11836153001]). Samples were centrifuged for 10 min at 12,000 ×
g
at 4°C. The supernatant was transferred to new tubes. All the SDS‐PAGE sample loading buffer was added to the protein lysates and boiled for 10 min at 95°C, and then examined by western blots with the indicated antibodies. Proteins were resolved by electrophoresis in SDS‐PAGE, blotted onto PVDF membranes, and blocked with 5% skimmed milk for 2 h at room temperature. Then the blocking buffer was removed and washed with TBST buffer for primary antibody incubation at 4°C overnight. After washing for 10 min 3 times, the membranes were incubated with the appropriate HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31430 and 31460) for 2 h at room temperature. The secondary antibodies were removed, and membranes were washed for 10 min with TBST 3 times. All bands were visualised in an ECL substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All the antibody information is shown in Table
S6
.
2.7
Animals
Animal experiments in this study were approved by and performed in accordance with the institutional animal care and use committee (IACUC) at the College of Life Science, Wuhan University (WDSKY0202008). Female NOD/SCID/IL2Rγ‐null (NSG) mice for 6–8 weeks were purchased from the Shanghai Model Organisms Centre (for sEV tail vein injection and MDA‐MB‐231 tumour models), female BALB/c mice for 6–8 weeks were purchased from the Centre for Disease Control (CDC, Hubei, China) (for 4T1 sEV tail vein injection, DPP3‐positive sEV chasing, and 4T1 xenograft model), and 6‐week‐old female BALB/c‐Nude mice purchased from GemPharmatech Corporation (for lung metastasis models) were used in this study. Mice were maintained under a cycle of 12 h light/12 h dark (on at 6:00/off at 18:00) with a temperature of 72°F ± 2°F and 30%–70% humidity and were allowed free access to food and water. For the orthotopic xenograft mice model establishment, MDA‐MB‐231 xenograft tumours were established by orthotopically injecting 2 × 10
5
Ctrl, 231/Rab27a‐KD or 231/DPP3‐KO cells mixed with Matrigel (Corning) into the fourth pair mammary fat pad. Similarly, 4T1 xenograft models were established by orthotopically injecting 2 × 10
5
of Ctrl, 4T1/Rab27a‐KO or 4T1/DPP3‐KO cells mixed with Matrigel (Corning) into the fourth pair mammary fat pad. The tumour volume was measured 10 days after tumour cell injection and was calculated using the formula (length × width
2
)/2. For sEV‐injected models, sEVs were intravenously injected into mice via the tail vein semiweekly for 5 weeks (∼10 µg sEVs per mouse), and mice were sacrificed 4 h after the last injection. For GW4869 and losartan treatment models, Balb/c mice bearing 4T1 tumours were administered GW4869 (10 mg/kg) or losartan (10 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal injection every other day, starting 2 weeks after tumour inoculation, and continued until mice were sacrificed. For the DPP3‐positive sEVs chasing
in vivo
, CFSE‐labelled 231/Ctrl sEVs and 231/DPP3‐ZsGreen sEVs (∼10 µg sEVs) were injected into mice via the tail vein, mice were sacrificed, and tissues were analysed by the IVIS Spectrum system (PerkinElmer) 4 h later. For the lung metastasis models, mice were pre‐educated by injecting sEVs via the tail vein semiweekly for 3 weeks (∼10 µg sEVs per mouse), and pre‐educated mice were injected with 1 × 10
6
MDA‐MB‐231‐luciferase cells via the tail vein. Three weeks later, lung metastasis was analysed by IVIS Spectrum system (PerkinElmer), and mice were sacrificed. For RAPGEF4 knockdown in lung tissues, AAV‐shRAPGEF4 virus or control virus was intratracheally instilled (1.5 × 10
13
genome copies suspended in 100 µL PBS was used per mouse) 1 week after implantation of 4T1 cells.
2.8
Micro‐PET/CT
Before the PET/CT was performed, mice were deprived of food overnight. The 18
F
‐FDG (5.5 MBq (150 µCi) in 0.1 mL) was injected into mice via the tail vein. One hour after 18
F
‐FDG administration, micro‐PET/CT imaging was performed. Micro‐PET/CT images were performed on a PET/CT scanner InliView‐3000B (Novel Medical, Beijing, China). While the micro‐PET/CT was imaging, all mice were subjected to isoflurane anaesthesia (1%–2% in 100% oxygen) and kept tight on a self‐adjust temperature tube to maintain body temperature throughout the procedure. Mice were visually monitored for breathing and any other signs of distress throughout the full imaging period. Data was analysed using the software NMSoft‐AIWS V1.7; the images were reconstructed using a three‐dimensional ordered subsets expectation maximum algorithm (OSEM) without attenuation correction. For data analysis, the region of interest (ROI) was manually drawn to cover the whole lung on fused images.
2.9
Bioluminescence Imaging (BLI)
BLI of the luciferase activity was used to indicate the metastasis progression of tumours. Before BLI was performed, the mice were administrated the injection of sodium pentobarbital (100 mg/kg) to anaesthetise and D‐luciferin potassium salt (150 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection to indicate the metastasis 10 min before imaging. After the whole‐body imaging, the lungs were collected in a 60 mm dish plate for bioluminescence imaging. Image exposure times were between 10 s and 1 min, depending on the signal strength. Light emission from the region of interest was quantified as photons s
−1
cm
−2
steradian
−1
.
2.10
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and Haematoxylin‐Eosin (H&E) Staining
Tissues were fixed in neutral formalin, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned into 5 µm sections. The IHC staining was performed using an IHC kit (ZSGB BIO, PV‐9000, China) according to the manufacturer's protocol. H&E staining was performed according to the standard procedure. All slides were scanned by an Aperio Versa slide scanner (Leica), and images were obtained using Aperio ImageScope software (Leica) and analysed by ImageJ. The immunohistochemical staining results of intensity were scored into four grades: 0, negative; 1, weak; 2, moderate and 3, strong. The frequency of positive cells was defined as follows: 0, less than 5%; 1, 5% to 25%; 2, 26% to 50%; 3, 51% to 75% and 4, greater than 75%. The intensity score was multiplied by the frequency score to obtain the final score. When the staining was heterogeneous, we scored it as follows: each component was scored independently and summed for the results.
2.11
Immunofluorescence (IF) and Multiplexed Immunofluorescence (mIHC)
For the IF staining of cultured cells, cells grown on the 0.1% gelatine (Solarbio, G8061) embedded coverslips (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were fixed with neutral paraformaldehyde for 30 min and washed with PBS. The slides were then blocked with 10% BSA at room temperature for 1 h after being permeabilised using 0.2% Triton X‐100 (Solarbio, T8200). For each antibody used, the cells were incubated at 4°C overnight and incubated with fluorescent‐conjugated secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature after being washed with PBS three times. After being sealed with an antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Beyotime, P0131), the slides were visualised by laser confocal microscopy (Leica SP8). The quantification of images was performed by ImageJ. For mIHC of tissues from patients and mice, a Panovue 4‐plex IHC kit (Panovue, 10001100020) was used. Briefly, 5 µm sections of FFPE tissues were cut and mounted on charged slides. Dewaxing and heat‐induced epitope retrieval of slides was performed using citrate antigen retrieval solution for 20 min at 100°C. Slides were further blocked with 10% w/v BSA in TBST. Antibodies were sequentially applied, followed by horseradish peroxidase‐conjugated secondary antibody incubation and tyramide signal amplification. Following labelling with TSA, antibodies were removed using a heat stripping step in citrate antigen retrieval solution for 10 min at 100°C. This step was not applied following the application of the third antibody. Slides were sealed with an antifade mounting medium with DAPI and scanned to obtain multispectral images using Thunder Imager DMi8 (Leica), and co‐localisations were analysed using LAS X software (Leica).
2.12
Tube Formation and Aortic Ring Sprout Assay and Permeabilisation of Mice Lungs
Tube formation and aortic ring sprouting assays were performed as previously described (Xu et al.
2021
). Pipette tips and a 96‐well plate used in this assay were precooled to −20°C. 50 µL Matrigel (ABW, 0827045) with a 1:1 dilution of FBS‐free DMEM was used to coat the plate well. 1 × 10
4
indicated sEVs pre‐treated HUVECs suspended in 100 µL of RPMI 1640 medium were seeded into the well. The formed tubes were observed and photographed by Olympus FluoView FV1000 and analysed by ImageJ after being incubated at 37°C after 6 h. For the aortic ring sprout assay, the thoracic aortas were obtained from 8‐week‐old female BALB/c mice. The fibro adipose tissue of the aortas was removed carefully, and the thoracic aortas were dissected into 1–2 mm rings. Pipette tips and a 96‐well plate used in this assay were precooled to −20°C. The aortic rings were embedded in the 1:1 diluted Matrigel in a 96‐well plate, and 100 µL RPMI 1640 medium was added into the wells. The medium in each well was replaced by 100 µL RPMI 1640 containing 0.2 µg indicated sEVs every 2 days. After 7 days of incubation at 37°C, the microvessels were photographed by Olympus FluoView FV1000 and analysed by ImageJ. To evaluate the vessels in the lungs, the lungs were permeabilised using the animal tissue optical clearing kit (Beyotime, P0112S) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, lung tissues were excised after mice were deeply anaesthetised and transcardially perfused with PBS, followed by 4% neutral paraformaldehyde. Then lungs were submerged in solution‐I and shaken in a 37°C incubator for delipidation for 2 weeks, CD31 (Proteintech, 28083‐1‐AP) antibody staining for 3 days at 37°C, and incubated with goat anti‐Rabbit IgG (H+L) Alexa 555 (Invitrogen, A‐21428) for 3 days at 37°C, and then RI matched with solution‐II in 37°C for 2 days. Tissues submerged in the mounting medium were visualised by the Leica lightsheet confocal microscope TCS SP8 DLS, and the number of branches in each field was quantified for further analysis.
2.13
RNA Sequencing and Pathways Analysis
RNA sequencing was conducted by Majorbio (Shanghai, China), and the transcriptome library was prepared using the TruSeq RNA Sample Preparation Kit from Illumina (San Diego, CA, USA), employing 1 µg of total RNA. Libraries were size selected for cDNA target fragments of 300 bp using 2% Low Range Ultra Agarose, followed by PCR amplification with Phusion DNA polymerase (NEB) for 15 PCR cycles. After being quantified using TBS380, the paired‐end RNA‐seq sequencing library was sequenced with the Illumina HiSeq X Ten/NovaSeq 6000 sequencer, which has a read length of 2 × 150 bp. The raw paired‐end reads underwent trimming and quality control using SeqPrep (
https://github.com/jstjohn/SeqPrep
) and Sickle (
https://github.com/najoshi/sickle
) with default parameters. Then, clean reads were separately aligned to reference genome with orientation mode using HISAT2 (
https://daehwankimlab.github.io/hisat2
) software. The mapped reads of each sample were assembled by StringTie (
https://ccb.jhu.edu/software/stringtie/index.shtml?%20t
= example) in a reference‐based approach. The expression levels of each transcript were calculated using the transcripts per million reads (TPM) method. RSEM (
http://deweylab.biostat.wisc.edu/rsem/
) was employed to quantify gene abundances. Finally, differential expression analysis was conducted with DESeq2. For the pathways analysis, GSEA (4.2.3) was used to identify pathway enrichment of the total genes expressed in the lungs of 231/Ctrl and 231/DPP3‐KO mice. The KEGG analysis was performed in the Metascape database (
https://metascape.org/gp/index.html#/main/step1
) using the significantly upregulated genes in 231/Ctrl lungs compared to the 231/DPP3‐KO group.
2.14
Luciferase Reporter Assays
Human RAPGEF4 promoter sequences were cloned into the pGL3‐basic luciferase vector. Luciferase assays were performed as previously described (Shen et al.
2017
). Briefly, cells were seeded in triplicate onto 24‐well plates and transfected with the indicated plasmids when cells reached ∼70% confluency. Forty‐eight hours after transfected, cells were harvested and lysed with 1× passive lysis buffer (PLB), and the luciferase activity was measured using the supernatant of cell lysate according to the manufacturer's instructions (Promega).
2.15
Chromatin Immunoprecipitation Assays and qPCR
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays were performed as previously described (Yu et al.
2024
). In brief, cells were transfected with Flag‐tagged YBX1 for 48 h and cross‐linked in situ with 1% formaldehyde for 10 min and then quenched with 0.125 M glycine for 5 min. The total cells were lysed with lysis buffer (50 mM Tris‐HCl, pH 8.0, 0.5% SDS, 5 mM EDTA). After centrifugation at 13,000 ×
g
, 4°C for 10 min, the samples were incubated in nuclei lysis buffer (50 mM Tris‐HCl (pH = 8.0); 10 mM EDTA; 1% Triton X‐100), then the cell was sonicated by bioruptor (Minichiller 300, Diagenode) with 30 cycles (30 s on, 30 s off). Then, the ChIP samples were incubated with Flag antibody (Sigma, F3165) and ChIP‐grade protein A/G magnetic beads (Thermo Scientific, 26162) at 4°C for 16 h. The beads were washed four times with wash buffer (250 mM LiCl, 10 mM Tris‐HCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% NP‐40, 1% sodium deoxycholate) and twice with elution buffer (10 mM NaHCO
3
, 1% SDS). The samples were finally de‐crosslinked at a temperature of 65°C for 16 h. DNA was purified using the Universal DNA Purification Kit (TIANGEN, DP214‐03) and analysed by RT‐qPCR with primers listed in Table
S5
.
2.16
Mass Spectrometry Analysis
For the ISGylation sites of DPP3 detection, the ISGylation system containing E1 (UBA7), E2 (UBE2L6), ISG15, and Flag‐tagged DPP3 was co‐transfected into HEK293T cells; cells were harvested after 48 h. For identifying potential proteins that interacted with DPP3 identification, MCF‐10A cells stably expressing the Flag‐tagged DPP3 were used for further analysis. Cells were harvested and lysed with NP‐40 buffer (50 mM Tris‐HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, EDTA, 1% Nonidet P‐40, phosphatase inhibitor, and protease inhibitor [Sigma, 11836153001]). After centrifugation at 12,000 ×
g
at 4°C for 10 min, the supernatant was collected and incubated with anti‐Flag antibody conjugated to magnetic beads and rotated at 4°C overnight. After SDS‐PAGE, bands were subjected to in‐gel trypsin digestion and dried. The composition of the protein was analysed by Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, San Jose, CA, USA) according to the protocols described previously (Shevchenko et al.
1996
).
For the detection of the sEV proteins via mass spectrometry, sEVs from MCF‐10A and MDA‐MB‐231 cell supernatant were extracted as mentioned. Mass spectrometry was performed at Beijing Proteome Research Centre using an LC‐MS/MS platform comprising a nanoflow high‐performance liquid chromatograph (HPLC) instrument (EASY‐nLC 1000 nanoflow LC, Thermo Scientific, USA) coupled with an LTQ Orbitrap Velos mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). Briefly, total protein was extracted from EVs by using the urea lysis buffer (6 M urea, 100 mM NH
4
HCO
3
, and 0.2% SDS) with protease inhibitor. Protein concentrations were detected with a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225). Following reduction, cysteine alkylation, and in‐gel digestion, samples were eluted using a 75 µm i.d. × 15 cm capillary column (Beijing SpectraPeaks) packed with 3 µm C18 reverse phase fused silica (Michrom Bioresources, Inc.). Eluting peptides were then analysed using the LTQ Orbitrap Velos mass spectrometer with a data‐dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. The raw data were analysed by MaxQuant software for protein identification and relative quantification.
2.17
Serum DPP3 Level Measurement
The whole blood samples of mice or humans were allowed to clot for 30 min at room temperature and then centrifuged at 3000 ×
g
for 30 min at 4°C to collect serum samples. The DPP3 level was measured by an enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit (mlbio, ml953302).
2.18
Protein Half‐Life Assays
Cells were transfected with the indicated vectors in 6‐well plates when they reached approximately 70% confluence. The protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX, 100 µg/mL) (MCE, HY‐12320) was used to treat for the indicated times after transfection. Cells were then harvested and analysed by immunoblotting with the indicated antibodies.
2.19
In Vivo Ubiquitination Assays
In vivo
ubiquitination assays were performed to detect the ubiquitination of the indicated proteins as previously described (Li et al.
2021
). Briefly, cells were transfected with the indicated plasmids. After 36 h, cells were treated with MG132 (20 µM) (MCE, HY‐1325) for 5 h before being harvested. Cells were lysed in 1 mL RIPA buffer, immunoprecipitated with indicated antibodies, and denatured by boiling for 5 min before immunoblotting. Immunoprecipitation and IB analysis were performed as described above.
2.20
Co‐Immunoprecipitation and Pull‐Down Assays
For the co‐immunoprecipitation (Co‐IP) assay, cells were harvested and lysed on ice with NP‐40 buffer for 1 h. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 ×
g
for 10 min, and 100 µL of supernatants were taken as input; the rest of the supernatants were subsequently incubated at 4°C overnight with magnetic beads labelled with the indicated antibodies. Beads were then washed five times with NP‐40 lysis buffer. Beads were suspended with 2 × loading buffer and boiled at 95°C for 10 min. For the pull‐down assays, the full length of human YBX1 was cloned into the pGEX‐6p‐1‐GST plasmid (Addgene, 274597‐01), and the human PFKP was cloned into pET‐28a. The BL21 (DE3) E. coli was transformed with the indicated vectors and cultured in LB medium. The proteins were then induced with IPTG (0.4 mM) for 4 h at 37°C when the OD
600
reached around 0.6. Proteins were purified using the GST‐Tag Protein Purification Kit with Magnetic Agarose Beads (Beyotime, P2260S) and NTA‐Ni Magnetic Agarose Beads for His‐Tag Protein Purification (Beyotime, P2241) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Equal amounts of purified GST‐tagged YBX1 with washed GST‐charged agarose beads (Beyotime, P2258) were incubated with equal amounts of His‐PFKP in pull‐down buffer (Tris‐buffered saline, TBS) and rotated at 4°C overnight. Similarly, an equal amount of purified His‐tagged PFKP with washed Ni‐charged magnetic beads (Beyotime, P2135) was incubated with an equal amount of GST‐YBX1 in pull‐down buffer (Tris‐buffered saline, TBS) and rotated at 4°C overnight. The beads were washed five times with wash buffer. The proteins were eluted from the beads by boiling with loading buffer, followed by immunoblotting analysis with the indicated antibodies.

The transcriptional factors binding to the RAPGEF4 promoter region were verified using the JASPAR database (
https://jaspar.elixir.no/

https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/

GSE165459

). The ssGSEA method was used to calculate DPP3 secretion scores of breast cancer cohorts in the TCGA database, with the expression of DPP3, ARF4 and ISG15 as the calculated markers. For the docking model, the structure of DPP3 (PDB ID: 5EGY) and ISG15 (PDB ID: 1Z2M) was obtained from the PDB database (

). The docking result shown in the figure was generated by PyMOL2.5.2.

Patient Cohorts
Serum samples from breast cancer patients and healthy donors and breast cancer tissues applied in this study were collected in accordance with the Clinical Research Ethical Committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University. All participants provided written informed consent. Paraffin‐embedded tissue sections and fresh tissues of breast cancer patients were obtained with voluntary patient consent from Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University. All the patient information was shown in Table

.

Statistical and Reproducibility
Statistical analysis was performed using the Prism 8 and R software (R version 4.3.2). All quantitative data are presented as mean ± SD. Two‐tailed Student's
t

r

1
Introduction
Breast cancer is among the most common malignancies and is the leading cause of cancer‐related death among women worldwide (Siegel et al.
2024
; Siegel et al.
2022
). Metastasis to distant organs is responsible for the majority of breast cancer‐related deaths (Bray et al.
2024
). The lungs, liver, bone and brain are the main targets of breast cancer metastasis, leading to poor patient outcomes (Bianchini et al.
2016
). The metastatic cascade involves multiple steps, including invasion, intravasation, circulation, extravasation and colonisation (Gerstberger et al.
2023
). Emerging evidence suggests that the primary tumour prepares various premetastatic niches (PMNs) in target organs before cancer cells spread from the initial site (Costa‐Silva et al.
2015
).
The vascular niche represents one of the predominant PMNs associated with lung metastasis in patients with breast cancer. Angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, is essential for remodelling the vascular niches in lung tissue and facilitating tumour cell colonisation (Kaplan et al.
2005
; Liu and Cao
2016
; Peinado et al.
2017
). Several pathways, including the Rap1 signalling pathway, regulate angiogenesis. The Rap1 signalling pathway affects multiple cancer‐related processes, such as proliferation, cell adhesion, inflammation and angiogenesis (Carmona et al.
2009
; Jang et al.
2012
; Lakshmikanthan et al.
2011
; Rothenberg et al.
2023
). RAP1A and RAP1B are two highly homologous Rap1 isoforms that act as molecular switches that regulate the activation of the Rap1 signalling pathway. This process is regulated by the GTP or GDP, which bind to Rap1, with GTP binding indicating ‘on’ and GDP binding indicating ‘off’ (Boettner and Van Aelst
2009
). This GTP‐binding process depends on the members of the Rap guanine nucleotide exchange factor (RAPGEF) family of proteins. RAPGEF4, also known as Epac2, regulates various physiological processes by activating the Rap1 signalling pathway, such as maintaining basal dendrites in mice and regulating insulin granule dynamics (Shibasaki et al.
2007
; Srivastava et al.
2012
).
Cancer cells communicate with specific target organs through the secretion of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), resulting in the formation of PMNs before metastasis (Ming et al.
2022
; Morrissey et al.
2021
; Wang et al.
2023
; Xu et al.
2021
; Xu et al.
2023
; Zhou et al.
2014
). Before cancer metastasis occurs, integrins on the surface of cancer cell‐derived sEVs guide them to the target organs (Ayuko et al.
2015
). Cargos in sEVs can educate immune or stromal cells to create the PMN through various pathways, such as MAPK/ERK, which facilitates metastasis (Jing et al.
2019
; Ming et al.
2022
; Qiu et al.
2022
; Samantha et al.
2021
; Xinrui et al.
2022
). Dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (DPP3) is an enzyme that cleaves bioactive peptides, and its dysfunction affects various physiological processes (Malovan et al.
2023
). Several studies have demonstrated that DPP3 targets and stabilises KEAP1 and CDK1 in breast cancer and colorectal cancer, assisting cancer cells in managing oxidative and cell cycle stress (Lu et al.
2017
; Tong et al.
2021
). ISGylation is a dynamic posttranslational modification (PTM) similar to ubiquitination, in which interferon‐stimulated gene 15 (ISG15) covalently attaches to target proteins through a sequential enzymatic process involving E1 (UBE1L), E2 (UBCH8) and E3 ligases (such as HERC5) (Han et al.
2018
). This process is triggered by interferon (IFN‐α/β/γ) responses to cellular stresses such as viral infections or oncogenic signalling. It influences various cellular functions, such as protein stability and subcellular localisation. Importantly, abnormal ISGylation has been linked to tumour progression through its ability to support cancer cell survival, metastasis, and immune system evasion (Yuan et al.
2023
). We previously reported that DPP3 can interact with and stabilise FASN, promoting fatty acid synthesis and breast cancer cell proliferation (Fu et al.
2024
). However, the function of DPP3 in metastasis remains unclear, and it is unknown whether DPP3 is modified by ISGylation and how such modification regulates its function.
In this study, we revealed that DPP3 packaged in sEVs secreted by breast cancer cells transcriptionally upregulates RAPGEF4 through the DPP3–PFKP–YBX1 axis. Elevated RAPGEF4 expression activates the Rap1 signalling pathway in lung endothelial cells, promoting angiogenesis and vascular niche remodelling, thereby facilitating lung metastasis in patients with breast cancer. Additionally, ARF4 recognises ISGylated DPP3 and transports it into sEVs. Pharmacologically blocking DPP3 ISGylation with losartan prevents its secretion and effectively decreases DPP3 accumulation in the lung tissue. Our findings revealed that cancer‐derived DPP3 functions as a key regulator of angiogenesis through the Rap1 signalling pathway and elucidates the mechanism through which proteins are packed into sEVs, providing valuable insights for the development of targeted strategies to diagnose and treat breast cancer metastasis.

Materials and Methods
2.1
Ethical Statement
This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations. Specifically, human specimens were obtained from Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University (Wuhan, China) and approved by the Clinical Research Ethical Committee of Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University in accordance with the principles of the Helsinki Declaration. Informed consent from all participants was obtained. All animal experiments were handled under the Guidelines of the China Animal Welfare Legislation and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the College of Life Science, Wuhan University.
2.2
Cells and Constructs
Cell lines, including MCF‐10A (CRL‐10317), MDA‐MB‐231 (HTB‐26), 4T1 (CRL‐2539) and HEK293T (CRL‐3216) used in this study, were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection and cultured in the recommended media or as indicated. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) were kindly gifted by Prof. Hanqiu Zheng (Tsinghua University). All cell lines were cultured in an atmosphere of 5% CO
2
in an incubator at 37°C. All cells used herein were tested to be free of mycoplasma contamination and authenticated using the short tandem repeat profiling method. Mycoplasma detection was tested by PCR with forward primer: 5’‐GGGAGCAAACAGGATTAGATACCCT‐3’ and reverse primer: 5’‐TGCACCATCTGTCACTCTGTTAACCTC‐3’ by MiniAmp thermocycler (Applied Biosystems, USA).
MCF‐10A cells were stably overexpressed with DPP3 (MCF‐10A/DPP3) or the empty PLVX‐IRES‐ZsGreen1 vector (MCF‐10 A/vec). MDA‐MB‐231/Lck‐GFP and MCF‐10A/Lck‐GFP cells were constructed by transfection of Lck‐GFP expression plasmid (Addgene #61099) and selected by G418 (Biofroxx, 1150GR001) and sorting of GFP
+
cells by flow cytometry. MDA‐MB‐231/Luciferase and 4T1/Luciferase cells were constructed by stably expressing plenti‐CMV‐Puro‐Luc (Addgene #17477) and selected by puromycin (BasalMedia, S250J0).
To construct knockdown cell lines, short hairpin RNA (shRNA) sequences targeted (Table
S8
) indicated genes were synthesised and cloned into pLKO.1 puro vector (Addgene, 8453). Cells were transduced by lentivirus and selected by puromycin (S250J0, Basal Media).
To knock out the DPP3 in MDA‐MB‐231 cells, using the CRISPR Cas9 genomic editing system, single‐guide RNA (DNA sequence GAAGGTGAGAACATCCAGGG) predicted by the CHOCHOP (
https://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/
) was synthesised in DNA form and annealed into double strands treated with T4 polynucleotide kinase and inserted into the lentiCRISPR‐v2 vector (Addgene, 52961). The constructed plasmid was transfected into MDA‐MB‐231 cells and selected by puromycin. Similarly, 4T1/DPP3‐KO cells using sgRNA (DNA sequence GCCGAGTGTTGTATGCACTG), 4T1/Rab27a‐KO cells using sgRNA (DNA sequence AGCGTCCCTGAAGAATGCAG). All knockout cell lines were screened by monoclonals and subsequently verified by Western blot.
As previously described (Wang et al.
2022
), the ZsGreen was added to the C‐terminal of DPP3 to construct the DPP3‐ZsGreen fusion protein. The DPP3 sequence and ZsGreen sequence were concatenated with the ScFv (Gly4Ser) x3 amino acid sequence coded by GGT GGA GGC GGT TCA GGC GGA GGT GGC TCT GGC GGT GGC GGA TCA as a linker.
To construct the reporters of YBX1‐mediated RAPGEF4 transcriptional regulation. The promoter region of human RAPGEF4 was cloned into the PGL3‐Basic reporter vector (Promega, Cat# E1751). P1 fragment using primers 5’‐TATGTTGCCCTGGCTGGTCT and 5’‐TGATTGCTGGTCAAGAACTA, P2 fragment using primers 5’‐CTGTAGTTCTTGACCAGC and 5’‐CCAAAAGCTTTCTGAAAATGC, P3 fragment using primers 5’‐TGACCTTGAAACATTCTCAGG and 5’‐CAGGCTGAAGTCACTGGC, P4 fragment using primers 5’‐GGGTCTCGGTTCTGCTGTGG and 5’‐GTTGAGCGGCGGCGCGCG and mutant of P1 (P1‐mut) fragment using primers 5’‐TCCCTAATCTACAGGACAGATCTATAGATTCGCTTTTTCTGGAAGTTTCAC and 5’‐AGCGAATCTATAGAtctgtcctgTAGATTAGGGATTGCCTAAGGCTGGG. For the overexpression vector construction, the human DPP3, YBX1, PFKP, UBA7, UBE2L6, USP18 and ISG15 were amplified from HEK293T cDNA and cloned into pLVX‐IRES‐ZsGreen1 and pLV3‐CMV‐MCS‐3×Flag‐Puro. Plasmids of potential ISGylation site mutants of human DPP3, dead mutants of human DPP3 and ISG15 and potential YBX1 binding site of RAPGEF4 promoter (P1‐mut) were created by site‐directed mutagenesis using 2×MultiF Seamless Assembly Mix (RM20523, ABclonal) according to the manufacturer's instructions. All plasmids were validated by sequencing (Quintarabio). All primer sequences for overexpression vector constructs are listed in Table
S4
.
2.3
Lentivirus Package
Plasmids such as shRNA, sgRNA or overexpression were transfected into HEK293T cells using Lipofectamine 2000 (Life Technologies) along with packaging plasmids: psPAX2 (Addgene, 12260) and pMD2.G (Addgene, 12259). Forty‐eight hours after transfection, the supernatant containing lentivirus was collected and filtered through a 0.45 µm filter. This filtered supernatant was then used to infect MCF‐10A, MDA‐MB‐231, 4T1 or HUVECs. The cells were incubated for 48 h in the presence of 10 µg/mL polybrene (Beyotime, C0351). Cells were selected based on puromycin or sorted by GFP
+
cells with FACS.
2.4
The sEV Isolation, Characterisation, Uptake and Treatment
The sEVs in the conditional medium were separated via ultracentrifugation as previously described (Yan et al.
2018
). Cells were cultured in an sEV‐free serum (prepared by ultracentrifugation serum at 100,000 ×
g
overnight [about 16 h] at 4°C) conditional medium, and the supernatant was collected and pre‐cleared by centrifugation at 500 ×
g
for 15 min and then at 10,000 ×
g
for 20 min. Eventually, the sEVs were isolated by ultracentrifugation at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min and then washed in PBS using the same ultracentrifugation conditions. The sEVs in the serum of mice or humans (breast cancer patients and healthy donors) were separated as previously described (Zhou et al.
2021
). The serum was diluted by an equal volume of PBS and centrifuged at 2000 ×
g
for 30 min at 4°C, followed by 12,000 ×
g
for 45 min at 4°C. Then, the supernatants were filtered through 0.22 µm filters (Millipore) and ultracentrifuged at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min at 4°C. The pellets were washed in PBS and subjected to a second ultracentrifugation step at 100,000 ×
g
for 70 min at 4°C. The mouse tumour‐derived sEVs were isolated following the protocol established previously (Hu et al.
2024
). Specifically, a ∼50‐mg piece of tumour was weighed and sliced on dry ice and then incubated in 100 U/mL collagenase type I in Hank's solution at 37°C. The dissociated tissue was spun at 300 ×
g
for 10 min at 4°C. The supernatant was transferred to a new tube and centrifuged at 2000 ×
g
for 15 min at 4°C. Cell‐free supernatant was filtered by a 0.22 µm filter gently and slowly to remove cell debris and spun at 10,000 ×
g
for 30 min at 4°C. The supernatants were ultracentrifugation at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min and resuspended in PBS for a second ultracentrifuged step at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min at 4°C.
OptiPrep (Sigma‐Aldrich, D1556) density gradient centrifugation was performed as previously described. EVs isolated by ultracentrifugation were loaded onto a 12‐step OptiPrep gradient consisting of 30%, 27.5%, 25%, 22.5%, 20%, 17.5%, 15%, 12.5%, 10%, 7.5%, 5% and 2.5% iodixanol in 20 mM Hepes (pH 7.2), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM Na
3
VO
4
and 50 mM NaF. After centrifugation in an SW 40 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter) at 110,000 ×
g
at 4°C for 16 h, twelve 1 mL fractions were collected and washed in PBS by another spin at 110,000 ×
g
for 70 min before western blot analysis (Yan et al.
2018
). EVs' size distribution was analysed using a CytoFLEX nanoFlow cytometer according to the manufacturer's instructions. The cytometer was calibrated for gating EVs with bead mixtures (Lot #2692902 and #BA105). About 10
9
particles/mL of fresh EVs were diluted 10,000‐fold in PBS. The report for particle size was generated directly from the CytExpert 2.2 software. The sEVs were negatively stained and characterised by transmission electron microscope (TEM). The sEVs were resuspended in 0.22 µm filters in PBS, gently dropped on the copper grids for 1 min, then stained using 2% uranyl acetate (SPI‐Chem, #02624‐AB) for 30 s at room temperature. The grids were examined by a JEOL JEM‐1400 Plus transmission electron microscope, and images were analysed by GATAN GMS 3 digital micrograph software.
For the sEVs uptake assay, sEVs extracted from each cell line were labelled with CFSE (eBioscience, 65‐0850‐84). CFSE was added to the PBS‐suspended sEVs at 5 µM and incubated for 1 h at room temperature before the washing step. This was followed by an extra round of ultracentrifugation washing in PBS to remove the excess dye. HUVECs were seeded into a 6‐well plate and incubated with CFSE‐labelled sEVs for 24 h. Images were acquired using the Leica DMi8.
For cell treatment, 2 µg of sEVs (equivalent to those derived from ∼5 × 10
6
parental cells) based on protein measurement using the BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added to 2 × 10
5
recipient cells in one well of a 6‐well plate. Cells treated with indicated sEVs were harvested after 24 h for RNA extraction and after 48 h for protein samples.
2.5
RNA Extraction and RT‐qPCR
Total RNA from cultured cells or tissues was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, 15596026) followed by cDNA synthesis using the MonScript RTIII Super Mix with dsDNase Kit (Monad Biotech, 509 MR05201). A CFX Connect real‐time PCR system (Bio‐Rad Laboratories) was used to perform quantitative real‐time PCR (RT‐qPCR) of cDNA samples using MonAmp ChemoHS qPCR Mix (Monad Biotech, MQ00401). All primers were designed using PrimerBank, and sequences are listed in Table
S5
.
2.6
Western Blots
Cells and sEVs were lysed in NP‐40 buffer (50 mM Tris‐HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, EDTA, 1% Nonidet P‐40, phosphatase inhibitor, and protease inhibitor [Sigma, 11836153001]). The mouse tissues (∼20 mg per sample) were ground with radioimmunoprecipitation assay buffer (50 mM Tris‐HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X‐100, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, sodium orthovanadate, sodium fluoride, EDTA and leupeptin, phosphatase inhibitor and protease inhibitor [Sigma, 11836153001]). Samples were centrifuged for 10 min at 12,000 ×
g
at 4°C. The supernatant was transferred to new tubes. All the SDS‐PAGE sample loading buffer was added to the protein lysates and boiled for 10 min at 95°C, and then examined by western blots with the indicated antibodies. Proteins were resolved by electrophoresis in SDS‐PAGE, blotted onto PVDF membranes, and blocked with 5% skimmed milk for 2 h at room temperature. Then the blocking buffer was removed and washed with TBST buffer for primary antibody incubation at 4°C overnight. After washing for 10 min 3 times, the membranes were incubated with the appropriate HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 31430 and 31460) for 2 h at room temperature. The secondary antibodies were removed, and membranes were washed for 10 min with TBST 3 times. All bands were visualised in an ECL substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All the antibody information is shown in Table
S6
.
2.7
Animals
Animal experiments in this study were approved by and performed in accordance with the institutional animal care and use committee (IACUC) at the College of Life Science, Wuhan University (WDSKY0202008). Female NOD/SCID/IL2Rγ‐null (NSG) mice for 6–8 weeks were purchased from the Shanghai Model Organisms Centre (for sEV tail vein injection and MDA‐MB‐231 tumour models), female BALB/c mice for 6–8 weeks were purchased from the Centre for Disease Control (CDC, Hubei, China) (for 4T1 sEV tail vein injection, DPP3‐positive sEV chasing, and 4T1 xenograft model), and 6‐week‐old female BALB/c‐Nude mice purchased from GemPharmatech Corporation (for lung metastasis models) were used in this study. Mice were maintained under a cycle of 12 h light/12 h dark (on at 6:00/off at 18:00) with a temperature of 72°F ± 2°F and 30%–70% humidity and were allowed free access to food and water. For the orthotopic xenograft mice model establishment, MDA‐MB‐231 xenograft tumours were established by orthotopically injecting 2 × 10
5
Ctrl, 231/Rab27a‐KD or 231/DPP3‐KO cells mixed with Matrigel (Corning) into the fourth pair mammary fat pad. Similarly, 4T1 xenograft models were established by orthotopically injecting 2 × 10
5
of Ctrl, 4T1/Rab27a‐KO or 4T1/DPP3‐KO cells mixed with Matrigel (Corning) into the fourth pair mammary fat pad. The tumour volume was measured 10 days after tumour cell injection and was calculated using the formula (length × width
2
)/2. For sEV‐injected models, sEVs were intravenously injected into mice via the tail vein semiweekly for 5 weeks (∼10 µg sEVs per mouse), and mice were sacrificed 4 h after the last injection. For GW4869 and losartan treatment models, Balb/c mice bearing 4T1 tumours were administered GW4869 (10 mg/kg) or losartan (10 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal injection every other day, starting 2 weeks after tumour inoculation, and continued until mice were sacrificed. For the DPP3‐positive sEVs chasing
in vivo
, CFSE‐labelled 231/Ctrl sEVs and 231/DPP3‐ZsGreen sEVs (∼10 µg sEVs) were injected into mice via the tail vein, mice were sacrificed, and tissues were analysed by the IVIS Spectrum system (PerkinElmer) 4 h later. For the lung metastasis models, mice were pre‐educated by injecting sEVs via the tail vein semiweekly for 3 weeks (∼10 µg sEVs per mouse), and pre‐educated mice were injected with 1 × 10
6
MDA‐MB‐231‐luciferase cells via the tail vein. Three weeks later, lung metastasis was analysed by IVIS Spectrum system (PerkinElmer), and mice were sacrificed. For RAPGEF4 knockdown in lung tissues, AAV‐shRAPGEF4 virus or control virus was intratracheally instilled (1.5 × 10
13
genome copies suspended in 100 µL PBS was used per mouse) 1 week after implantation of 4T1 cells.
2.8
Micro‐PET/CT
Before the PET/CT was performed, mice were deprived of food overnight. The 18
F
‐FDG (5.5 MBq (150 µCi) in 0.1 mL) was injected into mice via the tail vein. One hour after 18
F
‐FDG administration, micro‐PET/CT imaging was performed. Micro‐PET/CT images were performed on a PET/CT scanner InliView‐3000B (Novel Medical, Beijing, China). While the micro‐PET/CT was imaging, all mice were subjected to isoflurane anaesthesia (1%–2% in 100% oxygen) and kept tight on a self‐adjust temperature tube to maintain body temperature throughout the procedure. Mice were visually monitored for breathing and any other signs of distress throughout the full imaging period. Data was analysed using the software NMSoft‐AIWS V1.7; the images were reconstructed using a three‐dimensional ordered subsets expectation maximum algorithm (OSEM) without attenuation correction. For data analysis, the region of interest (ROI) was manually drawn to cover the whole lung on fused images.
2.9
Bioluminescence Imaging (BLI)
BLI of the luciferase activity was used to indicate the metastasis progression of tumours. Before BLI was performed, the mice were administrated the injection of sodium pentobarbital (100 mg/kg) to anaesthetise and D‐luciferin potassium salt (150 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection to indicate the metastasis 10 min before imaging. After the whole‐body imaging, the lungs were collected in a 60 mm dish plate for bioluminescence imaging. Image exposure times were between 10 s and 1 min, depending on the signal strength. Light emission from the region of interest was quantified as photons s
−1
cm
−2
steradian
−1
.
2.10
Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and Haematoxylin‐Eosin (H&E) Staining
Tissues were fixed in neutral formalin, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned into 5 µm sections. The IHC staining was performed using an IHC kit (ZSGB BIO, PV‐9000, China) according to the manufacturer's protocol. H&E staining was performed according to the standard procedure. All slides were scanned by an Aperio Versa slide scanner (Leica), and images were obtained using Aperio ImageScope software (Leica) and analysed by ImageJ. The immunohistochemical staining results of intensity were scored into four grades: 0, negative; 1, weak; 2, moderate and 3, strong. The frequency of positive cells was defined as follows: 0, less than 5%; 1, 5% to 25%; 2, 26% to 50%; 3, 51% to 75% and 4, greater than 75%. The intensity score was multiplied by the frequency score to obtain the final score. When the staining was heterogeneous, we scored it as follows: each component was scored independently and summed for the results.
2.11
Immunofluorescence (IF) and Multiplexed Immunofluorescence (mIHC)
For the IF staining of cultured cells, cells grown on the 0.1% gelatine (Solarbio, G8061) embedded coverslips (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were fixed with neutral paraformaldehyde for 30 min and washed with PBS. The slides were then blocked with 10% BSA at room temperature for 1 h after being permeabilised using 0.2% Triton X‐100 (Solarbio, T8200). For each antibody used, the cells were incubated at 4°C overnight and incubated with fluorescent‐conjugated secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature after being washed with PBS three times. After being sealed with an antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Beyotime, P0131), the slides were visualised by laser confocal microscopy (Leica SP8). The quantification of images was performed by ImageJ. For mIHC of tissues from patients and mice, a Panovue 4‐plex IHC kit (Panovue, 10001100020) was used. Briefly, 5 µm sections of FFPE tissues were cut and mounted on charged slides. Dewaxing and heat‐induced epitope retrieval of slides was performed using citrate antigen retrieval solution for 20 min at 100°C. Slides were further blocked with 10% w/v BSA in TBST. Antibodies were sequentially applied, followed by horseradish peroxidase‐conjugated secondary antibody incubation and tyramide signal amplification. Following labelling with TSA, antibodies were removed using a heat stripping step in citrate antigen retrieval solution for 10 min at 100°C. This step was not applied following the application of the third antibody. Slides were sealed with an antifade mounting medium with DAPI and scanned to obtain multispectral images using Thunder Imager DMi8 (Leica), and co‐localisations were analysed using LAS X software (Leica).
2.12
Tube Formation and Aortic Ring Sprout Assay and Permeabilisation of Mice Lungs
Tube formation and aortic ring sprouting assays were performed as previously described (Xu et al.
2021
). Pipette tips and a 96‐well plate used in this assay were precooled to −20°C. 50 µL Matrigel (ABW, 0827045) with a 1:1 dilution of FBS‐free DMEM was used to coat the plate well. 1 × 10
4
indicated sEVs pre‐treated HUVECs suspended in 100 µL of RPMI 1640 medium were seeded into the well. The formed tubes were observed and photographed by Olympus FluoView FV1000 and analysed by ImageJ after being incubated at 37°C after 6 h. For the aortic ring sprout assay, the thoracic aortas were obtained from 8‐week‐old female BALB/c mice. The fibro adipose tissue of the aortas was removed carefully, and the thoracic aortas were dissected into 1–2 mm rings. Pipette tips and a 96‐well plate used in this assay were precooled to −20°C. The aortic rings were embedded in the 1:1 diluted Matrigel in a 96‐well plate, and 100 µL RPMI 1640 medium was added into the wells. The medium in each well was replaced by 100 µL RPMI 1640 containing 0.2 µg indicated sEVs every 2 days. After 7 days of incubation at 37°C, the microvessels were photographed by Olympus FluoView FV1000 and analysed by ImageJ. To evaluate the vessels in the lungs, the lungs were permeabilised using the animal tissue optical clearing kit (Beyotime, P0112S) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, lung tissues were excised after mice were deeply anaesthetised and transcardially perfused with PBS, followed by 4% neutral paraformaldehyde. Then lungs were submerged in solution‐I and shaken in a 37°C incubator for delipidation for 2 weeks, CD31 (Proteintech, 28083‐1‐AP) antibody staining for 3 days at 37°C, and incubated with goat anti‐Rabbit IgG (H+L) Alexa 555 (Invitrogen, A‐21428) for 3 days at 37°C, and then RI matched with solution‐II in 37°C for 2 days. 3.1
DPP3 can be Encapsulated Into Breast Cancer sEVs and Accumulate in the Lungs
Cancer‐secreted sEVs play crucial roles in promoting tumourigenesis and metastasis through intercellular and interorgan crosstalk (Adem et al.
2024
; Hu et al.
2023
). To identify the proteins packaged in sEVs derived from breast cancer cells, we performed mass spectrometry (MS) with sEVs extracted from the triple‐negative breast cancer cell line MDA‐MB‐231 (231) and the normal breast epithelial cell line MCF10A (10A). DPP3 level was upregulated in sEVs derived from 231 cells compared to those derived from 10A cells (Figure
1a
). Furthermore, we detected higher DPP3 levels in 231‐derived sEVs than in 10A sEVs (Figure
1b
). The proteinase K treatment results suggest that DPP3 was carried in the lumen of the breast cancer sEVs (Figure
S1a
). In our previous work, we reported that DPP3 expression was significantly upregulated and strongly associated with poor prognosis in breast cancer patients (Fu et al.
2024
). However, the function of DPP3 packaged in sEVs remains largely unknown. Previous studies have shown that sEVs are pivotal in interorgan crosstalk (Adem et al.
2024
; Hu et al.
2023
). To evaluate whether sEVs from breast cancer containing DPP3 share similar functions, we constructed 231/Ctrl, 231/DPP3‐KO (knockout), and 231/Rab27a‐KD (knockdown) cell lines (Figure
S1b,c
). As a member of Rab‐GTPase, Rab27a has been reported to facilitate sEV secretion, with Rab27a knockdown significantly reducing sEV secretion in 231 cells (Figure
S1h,i
) (Iguchi et al.
2016
). These cell lines express membrane‐targeted Lck‐GFP, which anchors GFP to the sEV membrane, enabling
in vivo
tracking of sEVs. These cells were injected into the mammary fat pad of female NSG (NOD/SCID/ IL2Rγ‐null) mice to establish orthotopic xenograft models (Figure
1c
). Notably, DPP3 levels in serum and serum sEVs were higher in the 231/Ctrl group than in the tumour‐free, 231/DPP3‐KO and 231/Rab27a‐KD groups (Figure
1d,e
). These findings indicate that upregulated DPP3 in breast cancer cells can be encapsulated in sEVs and released into circulation.

3.2

Next, we aimed to explore the function of DPP3 accumulation in the lung tissues. RNA sequencing of lung tissues from mice bearing 231/Ctrl and 231/DPP3‐KO tumours was performed to investigate the function of DPP3. S2b–f
). DPP3 deletion mildly reduced the tumour volume in both the 4T1 and 231 models but had no observable effect on mouse body weight (Figure

3.3

We next investigated how circulating DPP3 promotes lung metastasis of breast cancer. GSEA enrichment analysis was performed using the RNA‐seq data of the lungs mentioned above. The angiogenesis pathway was significantly enriched in the lung tissues of the 231/Ctrl group compared with those of 231/DPP3‐KO (Figure
3a

2005

2018
). Intriguingly, compared with those in the tumour‐free, 231/DPP3‐KO, and 231/Rab27a‐KD groups, the CD105 signal in the lung tissues of mice bearing 231/Ctrl tumours was much stronger, with greater DPP3 accumulation (Figure

). Similarly, the intensity of CD105 staining was much greater in the lung tissues of mice bearing 4T1/Ctrl tumours compared to tumour‐free, 4T1/DPP3‐KO, and 4T1/Rab27a‐KO tumours (Figure
S3a,b
). Meanwhile, the intensity of CD105 staining in lung tissues from 4T1 sEVs‐injected mice was much higher than that of PBS‐injected mice (Figure
S3c,d
). Lung tissue is composed of numerous cell types, and previous studies have revealed that macrophages and endothelial cells play crucial roles in regulating angiogenesis (Corliss et al.
2016
; Xu et al.
2023
). We then explored whether macrophages or endothelial cells take up DPP3‐containing sEVs from breast cancer. IF images of lung tissues from mice injected with 231/DPP3‐ZsGreen sEVs revealed that endothelial cells, rather than macrophages, take up mainly DPP3‐positive sEVs (Figure

).

3.4

Our findings demonstrated that circulating DPP3 facilitated lung metastasis by promoting vascular formation in the lung. To elucidate the molecular mechanism by which DPP3 regulates angiogenesis, we performed Kyoto Encyclopaedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis using upregulated genes identified from RNA sequencing data of lung tissues from the 231/Ctrl group versus the 231/DPP3‐KO group. The results revealed significant enrichment of the Rap1 signalling pathway in the 231/Ctrl lung tissue samples (Figure

). 3.5

To investigate the underlying mechanism of RAPGEF4 regulation by DPP3, we first tested whether this process was affected by the enzyme activity of DPP3, which functions as a peptidase (Malovan et al.
2023
). We constructed an inactive mutant of DPP3, referred to as DPP3‐dead, by deleting the zinc‐binding motif 'HELLGH' amino sequence, which is responsible for the peptidase activity of DPP3 (Baral et al.
2008
). However, the DPP3‐dead mutant still upregulated RAPGEF4 levels in HUVECs (Figure
S5a
), indicating that the upregulation of RAPGEF4 expression is independent of the enzyme activity of DPP3.
We wondered whether a transcription factor (TF) targeted by DPP3 upregulates RAPGEF4 expression. Therefore, we overexpressed Flag‐tagged DPP3 in MCF‐10A cells and immunoprecipitated the Flag‐tagged DPP3 for MS to analyse potential DPP3‐interacting proteins. Intriguingly, YBX1, ZBTB43, PHB and CNBP were shown to interact with DPP3 on the basis of overlapping MS analysis data and all human TFs from the AnimalTFDB dataset (Figure

). Further verification using the JARSPAR database revealed that only YBX1 binds to the RAPGEF4 promoter region (Figure

). Co‐immunoprecipitation (Co‐IP) assays confirmed the interaction between YBX1 and DPP3 (Figure

), whereas IF assays revealed endogenous co‐localisation of YBX1 and DPP3 in HUVECs (Figure
S5b
). To assess the role of YBX1 in RAPGEF4 transcription, we measured the luciferase activity of RAPGEF4 promoter vectors containing wild‐type or mutant binding sites. YBX1 overexpression increased the luciferase activity of the WT RAPGEF4 promoter site (Figure
5d
). Furthermore, the ChIP‐qPCR results confirmed that, compared with the control sites 2# and 3#, YBX1 was enriched at the predicted binding site 1# (Figure
5e
). These data demonstrate that YBX1 binds to the RAPGEF4 promoter region. To further demonstrate that YBX1 is involved in the DPP3‐mediated regulation of RAPGEF4, DPP3 was ectopically overexpressed in HUVECs. IF revealed a significantly increased nuclear YBX1 ratio in DPP3‐overexpressing HUVECs (Figure
S5c
). Moreover, neither the mRNA nor the protein level of RAPGEF4 could be rescued in YBX1‐knockdown HUVECs despite DPP3 overexpression (Figure
S5d,e
).

Since sEV‐DPP3 derived from breast cancer cells promotes lung metastasis by stimulating angiogenesis, understanding how DPP3 is secreted is essential. We first determined which stage of endosomes is enriched in DPP3. IF assays showed the co‐localisation of DPP3 with RAB7 (an MVB marker) but not EEA1 (an early endosome marker), suggesting that DPP3 is directly sorted into MVBs (Figure
6a
). We found ADP‐ribosylation factor 4 (ARF4), a small GTPase reported to facilitate protein transport to late endosomes, which was identified in the DPP3 IP‒MS profile mentioned previously and may help with DPP3 packaging in MVBs (Figure
S6a
) (Rainero et al.
2015
). Co‐IP assays in 231 cells confirmed the endogenous interaction between DPP3 and ARF4 (Figure
S6b
). Furthermore, IF assays indicated that knocking down ARF4 in 231 cells blocked the co‐localisation of DPP3 and RAB7 (Figure
S6c
) and reduced DPP3 levels in sEVs (Figure
6b
). However, the exogenous interactions between DPP3 and ARF4 were not detected in HEK293T cells (Figure
S6d
). Therefore, we propose that factors may mediate the interaction between DPP3 and ARF4 in breast cancer cells. We identified interferon‐stimulated gene 15 (ISG15), a ubiquitin‐like protein that can be conjugated with other proteins as a modifier, in our DPP3 IP‒MS profile (Figure
S6e
). Previous studies have shown that ISG15 modification often occurs at protein‒protein interaction sites or at the dimerisation interface (Zhang et al.
2019
). Thus, we hypothesise that ISG15‐mediated ISGylation of DPP3 might serve as a molecular glue, facilitating the interaction between DPP3 and ARF4 and promoting DPP3 secretion.

Discussion
Breast cancer metastasis is the leading cause of breast cancer‐related death (Gerstberger et al.
2023
; Miller et al.
2019
; Siegel et al.
2024
). sEVs play a critical role in creating a premetastatic niche for tumour metastasis (Gerstberger et al.
2023
; Hoshino et al.
2020
; Nguyen et al.
2009
). Therefore, investigating the mechanisms through which sEVs promote cancer metastasis provides new insights and potential therapeutic targets.
Our current study demonstrated that DPP3 packaging in sEVs taken up by endothelial cells in lung tissues promotes angiogenesis by activating the Rap1 signalling pathway through RAPGEF4 via the DPP3–PFKP–YBX1 axis. DPP3, which is a peptidase, has been reported to degrade angiotensin
in vivo
, regulating renal heamodynamic and water homeostasis (Jha et al.
2020
; Picod et al.
2024
). Here, we show that DPP3 acts as a scaffold, recruiting PFKP to phosphorylate and stabilise YBX1, thereby increasing the transcription of RAPGEF4 in a peptidase activity‐independent manner, since inactivation of DPP3 did not prevent its ability to upregulate RAPGEF4 (Figure
S5a
).
In addition, PFKP, the rate‐limiting metabolic enzyme in glycolysis, directly alters glucose metabolism in cells (Mor et al.
2011
). Furthermore, PFKP has been reported to act as a scaffold to recruit AMPK to rescue glucose stress in NSCLC or to interact with c‐Myc to activate CXCR4 expression in leukaemia cell nuclei (Chen et al.
2022a
; Gao et al.
2021
). Similarly, in our study, PFKP, as a kinase, was found to be recruited by DPP3 to phosphorylate YBX1, preventing its polyubiquitination and subsequent degradation through the proteasome (Figure
5
). YBX1 is a nucleic acid‐binding protein that affects multiple processes, such as translation, RNA stability, mRNA splicing, and transcription (El‐Naggar et al.
2015
; Feng et al.
2021
; Jiang et al.
2022
; Perner et al.
2022
). In this study, YBX1 acts as a transcription factor and is translocated into the nucleus to increase RAPGEF4 expression (Figure
5
).
RAP1A and RAP1B are the core regulators of the Rap1 signalling pathway, as highlighted in previous research. However, in our study, the levels of RAP1A and RAP1B did not markedly change among the lung tissues from tumour‐free, 231/Ctrl, and 231/DPP3‐KO mice (Figure
S4c
). Interestingly, the expression of GTPase exchange factor 4 (RAPGEF4), which activates RAP1A/B, was notably elevated in the lung tissues of tumour‐bearing mice and mice treated with DPP3‐enriched sEVs (Figure
4b‐e
). This phenomenon was also observed in sEV‐treated HUVECs (Figure
S4g
). Elevated RAPGEF4 activates the Rap1 signalling pathway, subsequently promoting angiogenesis, remodelling vascular niches in the lung, and increasing breast cancer metastasis.
Emerging evidence has shown that sEVs are key mediators of metastasis progression. Cargo in sEVs is selectively packaged during their biogenesis. The endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) is the main mechanism that facilitates the sEV production and the selective sorting of ubiquitin‐modified proteins into them (Katzmann et al.
2001
; Raiborg and Stenmark
2009
). LAMP2A identifies proteins that contain ‘KFERQ’ peptides and facilitates their sorting into sEVs in a manner that is independent of the ESCRT pathway (Ferreira et al.
2022
). Our study revealed that ADP‐ribosylation factor 4 (ARF4), a member of the small GTPase family involved in vesicle transport, is associated with and transports DPP3 into MVBs to promote its secretion. Previous studies have shown that ARF4 facilitates the transport of Golgi vesicles to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to promote breast cancer cell growth and invasion (Howley et al.
2018
). Additionally, ARF4 regulates the internalisation of integrin α5β1 and its trafficking into endosomes (Rainero et al.
2015
). Interferon (IFN)‐stimulated gene 15 (ISG15), which is critical in multiple pathological processes such as antiviral immunity and tumour progression, is primarily stimulated by type‐I IFN. ISG15 and ISGylation affect diverse cancer cell processes and can also be induced by IFNγ (Niu et al.
2015
). Our study revealed that DPP3 was ISGylated, enabling ARF4 to recognise and package it into MVBs for subsequent secretion. These findings suggest that ISGylation may regulate cargo packaging during sEV biogenesis. Targeting this process could be an effective strategy for cancer treatment. We found that losartan treatment reduced IFNα‐induced ISGylation, prevented DPP3 secretion via sEVs, and decreased DPP3 accumulation in lung tissue (Figure
S7j–m
). In our study, we observed that DPP3‐positive sEVs were specifically absorbed by lung tissues. Previous studies have confirmed that integrins on the surface of sEVs—such as ITGB4‐, ITGA6‐ and ITGB1‐positive sEVs, which are specifically absorbed by lung tissue—determine their organotropism (Ayuko et al.
2015
). An interaction between ITGB4 and DPP3 was identified in our IP‐MS profile (data not shown), which may explain the lung‐specific uptake of DPP3‐positive sEVs. This mechanism needs further investigation.
In conclusion, our study revealed that breast cancer cells secreted DPP3 via sEVs, which were delivered to endothelial cells in lung tissue. This activates the Rap1 signalling pathway by transcriptionally upregulating RAPGEF4 via the DPP3–PFKP–YBX1 axis, promoting angiogenesis and breast cancer lung metastasis. Additionally, ISG15‐mediated ISGylation is a key regulator of DPP3 packaging into sEVs (Figure
8
). Our findings provide a deeper understanding of how breast cancer spreads to the lung through the remodelling of vascular niches and reveal a mechanism for cargo packaging into sEVs, positioning DPP3 as a potential new target for breast cancer treatment.
